latin.200: Posterior quaestio de hujus peccati imputati poena etiam ipsa aliquam explicationem desiderat. Primum autem poena distinguenda est; deinde separandus a nobis Adamus. Poena dicitur vel proprie, vel improprie. Proprie rursus multipliciter: sed nihil opus est omnia poenarum genera quae te nosse arbitror, enumerare, id enim cum longum esset, tum ad rem quam agimus inutile. Satis est tenere quo sensu corruptio haereditaria poena dicatur a te aliisque fratribus nostris, quorum sententiam adversus me tueri vis.
latin.201: Nempe statuis esse poenam strictissime ac propriissime sic dictam, cujus hae sunt conditiones. 1. Lex eam comminatur. 2. Iustitia ut infligatur a Iudice exigit. 3. Iudex eam infligit ut fiat iustitia, sive ut iustitiae satisfiat. Itaque Ursinus in explicat. Catechet. Cum sibi objecisset non debuisse Deum culpam Adami tali poena punire, respondit fiat iustitia & pereat Mundus.
latin.202: Ego vero talem esse poenam & negavi in Thesibus & non possum impetrare a conscientia mea ut nunc quoque non negem. Scio hanc corruptionem seu concupiscentiam poenam a Patribus appellari, necnon alicubi a Calvino, sed nego sensu ita proprio, ita stricto. Sed ob similitudinem quandam poenae nomen ei accommodatur. Ut enim poena sequitur culpam & cum ea cohaeret, sic corruptio haereditaria secuta est culpam Adami atque ex ea nata est.
latin.203: Ut non est in ejus qui punitur potestate poenam admittere, vel non admittere aut etiam excutere, sic ab alio corruptione ista afficimur, nec in nobis situm est eam non admittere, aut excutere. Ut poena ejus cui infligitur conditionem mutat in deteriorem, sic hac corruptione inquinatus Adamus deterior, ignobilior, foedior, miserior, quam alioqui fuisset, evasit.
latin.204: Denique ut qui inflictam poenam sentit, ingemiscit, & ab ea liberari percupit; sic qui hanc in se corruptionem deprehendunt & agnoscunt serio, vehementer indolescunt & aegre ferunt se hujus mali vinculis illigari. Has ob similitudines merito tetrum istud & horrendum malum poena dici potuit & dicitur a multis.
latin.205: Sed quaeritur inter nos duntaxat, num sit poena sensu illo, quem explicavi, maxime proprio & stricto. Has duas quaestiones, quia tu non separasti, ut feret occasio, tua sequens vestigia, Deo favente, tractabo.

pass_a.200: The posterior question concerning the penalty of this imputed sin itself also desires some explanation. First, however, penalty must be distinguished; then Adam must be separated from us. Penalty is said either properly or improperly. Properly again in many ways: but there is no need to enumerate all the kinds of penalties which I think you know, for that would be both long and useless to the matter we are treating. It is enough to hold in what sense hereditary corruption is called a penalty by you and by our other brothers, whose opinion you wish to defend against me.
pass_a.201: Namely you establish that it is a penalty in the strictest and most proper sense so called, whose conditions are these. 1. The Law threatens it. 2. Justice requires that it be inflicted by the Judge. 3. The Judge inflicts it that justice may be done, or that justice may be satisfied. Thus Ursinus in the Catechetical Explanation. When he had objected to himself that God ought not to have punished the fault of Adam with such a penalty, he answered let justice be done and the World perish.
pass_a.202: But I denied that it is such a penalty in the Theses, and I cannot obtain from my conscience that I should not deny it even now. I know this corruption or concupiscence is called a penalty by the Fathers, and also somewhere by Calvin, but I deny it in a sense so proper, so strict. But on account of a certain likeness the name of penalty is accommodated to it. For as penalty follows fault and coheres with it, so hereditary corruption followed the fault of Adam and was born from it.
pass_a.203: As it is not in the power of him who is punished to admit the penalty, or not admit it, or even to shake it off, so we are affected by that corruption from another, and it is not situated in us not to admit it, or to shake it off. As the penalty of him on whom it is inflicted changes the condition into a worse, so Adam stained by this corruption became worse, more ignoble, fouler, more miserable, than he otherwise would have been.
pass_a.204: Finally as he who feels the inflicted penalty groans and earnestly desires to be freed from it, so those who seriously detect and acknowledge this corruption in themselves vehemently grieve and bear with difficulty that they are bound by the chains of this evil. For these likenesses that foul and horrible evil deservedly could be called and is called a penalty by many.
pass_a.205: But it is asked among us only whether it is a penalty in that sense which I explained, most proper and strict. These two questions, because you did not separate them, that opportunity may arise, following your footsteps, God favoring, I will treat.

200: Before we go further, the later question on the penalty tied to this imputed sin needs clearing. Two moves first: sort out what penalty means, and keep Adam distinct from us. Penalty can be named properly or improperly, and even the proper sense branches many ways. I will not catalogue every species you already know—that would be long and beside our point. Hold only the sense in which you and the other brothers whose case you defend against me call hereditary corruption a penalty.
201: On your account this is penalty in the tightest proper sense, and you put three marks on it. The Law must threaten it. Justice must demand that the Judge lay it on. The Judge must lay it on so justice is done—or so justice is satisfied. Ursinus, in the Catechetical Explanation, faced the objection that God should not have punished Adam with such a penalty, and answered: Let justice be done, though the world perish.
202: In the Theses I refused to count it that sort of penalty, and conscience still will not let me reverse that denial. The Fathers do call this corruption—or concupiscence—a penalty, and Calvin does in places; I do not deny the word, only the so-proper, so-strict sense. The name rides on likeness. Penalty tracks fault and clings to it; hereditary corruption likewise tracked Adam's fault and sprang from it.
203: A punished person cannot choose to take the penalty, refuse it, or cast it off. We are hit by this corruption from another in the same way: refusing or casting it off is not in our power. A penalty also worsens the state of the one it strikes. Stained by this corruption, Adam became worse—more ignoble, fouler, more wretched—than he would have been without it.
204: Last likeness: whoever feels a penalty laid on groans and longs for release. Those who seriously find and own this corruption in themselves likewise grieve hard and hate being chained by that evil. For such likenesses many writers have rightly named—and still name—that foul, dreadful evil a penalty.
205: Among us the sole live question is whether it is penalty in that most proper, strict sense I just marked out. You did not keep the two questions apart. God willing, I will take them up in turn as the chance comes, following your own steps.
